pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–8 years

- **Topic:** Comparing Design Solutions

- **Standards — US (NGSS K–2-ETS1-3, Engineering Design):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-2-ETS1-3]. This is the data-and-evidence engineering-design performance expectation at the K–2 band, drawing on SEP 4 (Analyzing and Interpreting Data).

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS1 Design & Technology — Evaluate; Working Scientifically):** Pupils should be taught to evaluate their ideas and products against design criteria, and (in science) to perform simple tests and use observations to answer questions. Testing two solutions and using the results to judge which works better combines the D&T 'evaluate' skill with the science 'gather and use data' skill.

- **Operational details:** The child tests TWO designs that tackle the same problem (two paper-bridge shapes; two boat hulls; two shade structures), gathers simple performance data on each (how much weight held, how far it went, how cool it stayed), and then COMPARES the results to name each design's strengths and weaknesses — finally using the data as evidence to recommend which works better and to suggest an improvement. The key move beyond a single test is evidence-based comparison: the recommendation must rest on what the numbers/observations showed, not on which design the child liked or made. This begins to fuse the doing (testing), the recording (data), and the arguing (evidence-based judgement) strands.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A–B (concrete, early evidence-use). This is the first time data is used to judge between competing designs — the root of design comparison and evidence-based evaluation. Success = tests two designs for the same problem, records how each performed, and uses that evidence to say which is better and why, naming a strength and a weakness of each.
bestPractices: Test both designs the SAME way (same load, same drop) so the comparison is fair and the data is meaningful.
Record each design's performance simply (a number, tally or mark) so the comparison rests on evidence, not memory or preference.
Draw out strengths AND weaknesses of each design, so children see trade-offs rather than a single 'winner'.
Insist the recommendation cite the data ('the arch held more bricks') rather than 'I like it / I made it'.
Follow the comparison with a 'how could we improve it?' step, seeding iteration.
Use problems where each design wins on a different measure, so comparison becomes multi-dimensional.
keyRepresentations: Two designs tested the same way on a shared problem
Side-by-side results chart (Design A vs Design B)
Evidence-based recommendation ('better because the data showed…')
An improvement note for the chosen design
commonMisconceptions: Recommending the design you liked or built rather than the one the data supports.
Testing the two designs differently, making the comparison unfair.
Seeing only a 'winner' and missing that each design has strengths and weaknesses.
Judging on appearance rather than measured performance.
Not recording results, so the comparison rests on memory or feeling.
Thinking the better design needs no improvement.

learn.summary: For ages 5–8, teach evidence-based comparison of two engineering designs that solve the same problem: test both the SAME way, record each one's performance, then recommend the better-performing design by citing the recorded data (not preference or looks), name a strength AND weakness of each, and suggest one improvement. The central move beyond a single test is that the recommendation must rest on what the numbers/observations showed. The same test–record–compare loop works with other same-problem contexts (two bridge shapes, two boat hulls, two shade structures). The strongest version has children generate the head-to-head data through their own fair tests; pre-authored scenes, dialogue, and scored questions can support interpretation and vocabulary but do not let the child produce the comparison themselves.

activities.title: Best Design Wins: testing two bridges with a shared load
feedback: If a winner is named before both are tested, withhold the verdict: 'What did the bricks actually show for each one?' Anchor the decision to the results, not the look.
If nothing is written down, prompt recording each trial as it happens so the comparison is a matter of reading the record, not recalling it.
If the two designs were handled differently (different gap, dropping vs placing weights, unequal time), ask the child to state what was kept the same, then re-run so only the design differs.
If only a single 'winner' is seen, prompt: 'this one held more — but which was quicker to build? which used less material?' so the other design can earn a strength too.

If the shade context is used, keep conditions fair (same spot, same exposure time) and judge the result by the shadow or transmitted light patch on the ground over equal elapsed time — never by looking at the sun through a cover; shade reduces warming over time rather than cooling a hot spot instantly.
activities.rationale: The objective is a test–record–compare loop the child runs themselves, so the evidence-over-preference lesson is felt through their own data rather than read off a finished chart. A live scoreboard that fills as each test runs can make the data visibly come from the child's actions; these are illustrative interaction examples, not required mechanisms.
sourceClaims: NGSS K–2-ETS1-3 requires students to [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-2-ETS1-3].

DfE KS1 Design & Technology requires pupils to evaluate their ideas and products against design criteria; KS1 science Working Scientifically requires performing simple tests and using observations to answer questions.
learnerActions: Set up two designs for the same problem — e.g. a flat bridge and an arched bridge made from the same material and spanning the same gap (or, as alternatives, two boat hulls floated the same way, or two shade structures compared by how much light gets through — judged by the cast shadow or transmitted light patch on the ground — and/or by how cool the shaded spot stays, checked with a thermometer or hand touch over the same time; never by looking toward the sun or holding material up to the eyes).
State out loud what you will keep the same for both (same gap, same way of adding weight, same exposure time) before you start, so the test is fair.
Add weights (toy bricks or marbles) to the first design one at a time, and record the number it held before it sagged or dropped (e.g. flat bridge held 8).
Test the second design exactly the same way and record its number (e.g. arch held 12).
Fill both numbers into a side-by-side comparison chart (Design A row vs Design B row).
Recommend which design performed better and point to the recorded numbers as your reason.
Say one way you would improve the weaker design, linked to why it underperformed.
activities.intendedInsight: The recorded data — not your favourite or the one you built — shows which design performed better on the measure you tested, and you can point to the numbers to prove it.

activities.title: Trade-offs: when each design wins on a different measure
feedback: If the child only tracks one measure, add the second measure and ask which design wins on each.
If they insist one design is best at everything, point to the record showing the other's strength.
If the recommendation ignores purpose, ask 'better for what — holding weight, or being quick to build?'
activities.rationale: Comparison becomes multi-dimensional when each design wins on a different measure, moving children past a single-winner view toward naming strengths and weaknesses on both sides.
sourceClaims: NGSS K–2-ETS1-3 requires students to [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-2-ETS1-3].
learnerActions: Choose a problem where each design can win on a different measure — e.g. one bridge holds more weight but the other is quicker to build or uses less paper.
Test and record each design on BOTH measures (e.g. weight held, and time or material used).
Tag each design with a strength and a weakness based on the records.
Explain why there is no single 'best' — each design has trade-offs — and recommend one for a stated purpose, citing which measure mattered most.
activities.intendedInsight: Real designs have trade-offs: one design can be strong on one measure and weak on another, so the recommendation depends on which measure matters for the problem.

activities.title: Read the results chart and defend the pick (interpretation practice)
feedback: If a 'liked it more' option is chosen, ask what the table actually shows before deciding.
If a design is called the winner on appearance, redirect to the measured numbers in the table.
When a correct pick is made, prompt the child to name a weakness of the chosen design too, so trade-offs stay visible.
activities.rationale: Interpreting a given results table and distinguishing evidence from preference builds the vocabulary and reasoning of comparison; offering a tempting option for the design the learner liked more probes the evidence-over-preference idea directly. This is recognition/interpretation practice and does not have the child run the tests or build the comparison.
sourceClaims: NGSS K–2-ETS1-3 requires students to [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-2-ETS1-3].
learnerActions: Look at a small side-by-side results table for two designs tested on the same problem.
Decide which design the data supports as better for the stated problem.
Reject a 'liked it more' or 'looks stronger' reason and give the data-based reason instead.
Match each design to its strength and its weakness from the table; sort listed features into strengths vs weaknesses.
activities.intendedInsight: An evidence-based recommendation reads the recorded results and names strengths and weaknesses, rather than relying on appearance or preference.

activities.title: Justify-it dialogue: pressing for evidence and a weakness
feedback: If the justification is 'I like it' or 'I made it', press: 'what in the results shows that?'
If only strengths are given, ask for a weakness of the chosen design.
If the child can't say how to retest an improvement, prompt: 'how would we test whether your change actually helped?'
activities.rationale: Spoken justification reinforces evidence-based judgement and surfaces trade-offs through responsive questioning. It depends on the child having already run and seen the two tests, so dialogue supports rather than leads the comparison.
learnerActions: After running the two tests, answer a prompt like 'the data shows A held more — so which do you recommend, and what's a weakness of A?'
Point to the specific result that supports the recommendation.
Name a weakness of the design you chose, not just its strength.
Answer a follow-up on how you'd check your improvement actually helped.
activities.intendedInsight: A good recommendation can be defended by pointing to evidence and still acknowledges the chosen design's weaknesses.

constraints: Both designs must be tested the SAME way (same kind of weights, same gap, same way of adding weight, same exposure time where time matters) so the comparison is fair and the data is meaningful.
Record each design's performance simply — a number, tally or mark — so the comparison rests on evidence, not memory or preference.
Draw out strengths AND weaknesses of each design so children see trade-offs, not just a single winner.
The recommendation must cite the data (e.g. 'the arch held more bricks'), not 'I like it' or 'I made it'.
Follow the comparison with a 'how could we improve it?' step to seed iteration.

Interpretation/recognition tasks (reading a given table, matching, sorting features) check the judgement but do not elicit the child running the two tests and building the comparison, which is the core objective; use them as supports, not substitutes.
A pre-authored tap-to-reveal comparison scene can teach the vocabulary but does not have the child generate the head-to-head data from their own testing.
Dialogue prompts are designed to follow the child having run and seen both tests; use them alongside, not instead of, the hands-on comparison.
Keep the better-design message honest: the recommended design can still be improved — avoid implying the winner needs no change.

If a shade structure is used as the problem, observe safely: inspect the cast shadow or the transmitted light patch on the ground (or measure how cool a spot stays) over equal elapsed time; never ask a child to look at the sun through a cover or hold material up toward the sun. Shade reduces warming under fair conditions rather than cooling a hot spot instantly, and mesh may partially reduce warming depending on weave — compare actual outcomes, do not predetermine a winner.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; both listed sources carry verified:false in the row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Physical results depend on build quality and materials (e.g. an arch is not guaranteed to outperform a flat bridge); the 8-vs-12 brick figures are illustrative examples, not expected outcomes. Treat observed numbers from the child's own test as the evidence, whatever they are.

Shade comparisons reduce solar warming under fair conditions; outcomes should be compared with equal elapsed time and conditions, observing the shadow/transmitted patch on the ground rather than looking toward the sun. Mesh or thin covers may partially reduce warming depending on weave and setup; do not assume mesh fails or an opaque cover instantly cools.

The legacy row claimed 3D 'adds navigation cost without sharpening' the idea and that scored quizzes 'can't' carry the core; these are reframed as scoped affordance/limit notes — a 3D physical test or a quiz can still contribute, they just do not replace child-run fair testing.
The 'test again tomorrow — same result?' probe is a good reliability idea but may exceed some 5-year-olds; keep it optional/extension.
Alternative concrete problem contexts (two boat hulls, two shade structures) from the original are retained as substitutes for the bridge scenario.

probeDeeper: Your record shows one held more marbles — what was it about that design that made it stronger?
You changed one thing to improve the weaker bridge — how would we test whether your change actually helped?
If we tested them again tomorrow, do you think we'd get the same result? How could we be more sure?
assess.correctAnswer: The child tests both bridges under the same conditions, records each one's performance (e.g. marbles held before collapse), compares the recorded results to name each design's strength and weakness, and recommends the better design by pointing to the data — then suggests an improvement tied to why the weaker one failed.

errorPatterns.pattern: Judges by appearance or preference rather than by how each performed in the test ('the blue one looks stronger, it wins').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Withhold the verdict until both are tested; ask 'what did the marbles actually show?' Anchor the decision to the results, not the look.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Announces a winner based on looks or a favourite, sometimes before finishing the tests.

errorPatterns.pattern: Doesn't record results — relies on memory, so the comparison can't be justified with data.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist on recording each trial as it happens; then the comparison is a matter of reading the record, not recalling it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Tests both but writes nothing down; when asked which was better, guesses or misremembers the counts.

errorPatterns.pattern: Tests the two designs under different conditions (different gap, dropping marbles vs placing them), so the comparison isn't fair.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have the child state what they kept the same for both before testing; re-run so only the design differs.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Handles each bridge differently; the two tests aren't comparable.

responseLevels.gap: Picks a winner by looks or preference; tests unequally or not at all; no record of results.
responseLevels.full: Tests both fairly, records each one's performance, recommends the better design by citing the data, and suggests an improvement linked to why the other underperformed.
responseLevels.partial: Tests both and records something, but the comparison is loose — tests aren't quite fair, or the recommendation isn't clearly tied to the recorded data.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are two paper bridges that were built to solve the same problem: hold as many marbles as possible across this gap. Test both, keep a record of how each one does, and then tell me which design is better and why — and one thing you'd change to improve it. (Provide the two bridges, marbles, and a way to record; watch how the child tests and what they base the verdict on.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Only watching shows whether the verdict rests on evidence: a child who understands tests both the same way, writes the numbers down, and cites them; a child who doesn't judges by appearance, tests them differently, or relies on memory. Asking 'how do you compare designs?' wouldn't reveal that they actually declared a winner before testing.
